A precision-recall curve is a classifier's precision against its recall, one
point per decision threshold. scikit-learn draws one with
`PrecisionRecallDisplay`, and every way of building that display --
`from_estimator`, `from_predictions`, `from_cv_results`, or a display built by
hand -- ends in its `plot()`, which is what maidr reads.

Read as a plain step line, a precision-recall curve answers the wrong
questions. Whether a classifier beats guessing is how far its precision sits
above the share of positives in the data -- a level that is different for
every dataset -- and the average precision the chart is quoted by sits in the
legend text, where a screen reader user is never told it. maidr reads the
display instead: each point announces how far its precision sits above that
baseline, and the description gives the average precision of each curve
against it and the point with the best F1 score.

`PR_CURVE` is **experimental** and may change without a deprecation period:
see [Plot Type Stability](../stability.qmd).

::: {.callout-warning title="Prototype"}
This is one of the experimental plot types. It has not been through a user
study, and it may change without a deprecation period. See
[Plot type stability](../stability.qmd).
:::

## Setup

The examples on this page need scikit-learn, which is an optional extra:
`pip install maidr[sklearn]`. Nothing in maidr imports it; the reading is
wired up when your own code imports `sklearn.metrics`.

```{python}
#| warning: false

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Just import maidr package: plt.show() now renders accessible output #<<
import maidr  #<<
```

## One classifier

```{python}
#| warning: false
#| fig-alt: Precision-recall curve of a logistic regression classifier, with the chance level dashed

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import PrecisionRecallDisplay
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

import maidr  #<<

X, y = make_classification(
    n_samples=600, n_informative=4, weights=[0.8], random_state=0
)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=0)
model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=500).fit(X_train, y_train)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
# The display's own plot() is what maidr reads. The dashed chance level it
# draws is a reference, not a curve: maidr reads every point against it.
PrecisionRecallDisplay.from_estimator(  #<<
    model, X_test, y_test, ax=ax, plot_chance_level=True  #<<
)  #<<
ax.set_title("Precision-recall curve of a logistic regression")

plt.show()  #<<
```

The curve is one series: Left and Right move along it from low recall to high,
and each stop announces the recall, the precision and how far the precision
sits above the share of positives -- about one in five here, since the data is
imbalanced. The description (`d`) gives the average precision, which is the
number the display computed, against that baseline, and the point with the
best F1 score.

## Comparing classifiers

Two displays plotted on one axes are two curves of one chart, so Up and Down
switch between classifiers at the same recall.

```{python}
#| warning: false
#| fig-alt: Precision-recall curves of a logistic regression and a random forest on one axes

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import PrecisionRecallDisplay
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

import maidr  #<<

X, y = make_classification(
    n_samples=600, n_informative=4, weights=[0.8], random_state=0
)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=0)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for model in (LogisticRegression(max_iter=500), RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0)):
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    PrecisionRecallDisplay.from_estimator(model, X_test, y_test, ax=ax)  #<<
ax.set_title("Precision-recall curves of two classifiers")

plt.show()  #<<
```

Each curve is named the way the caller named it -- the estimator's class here,
or the `name=` passed to the display -- rather than by the legend entry, which
wraps the average precision around the name. The description lists the
average precision of every curve and names the highest.

## Drawn by hand

A curve drawn straight from `precision_recall_curve` with `ax.plot()` or
`ax.step()` is read the same way when its axes are titled exactly `Recall`
and `Precision` and every value is a fraction of one: those titles are what
says the line is a precision-recall curve. It carries no share of positives,
so its points are not read against a baseline; the average precision is
measured from the points. A plotly line, or the `px.area(x=recall,
y=precision)` plotly's own documentation draws, is read the same way under
the same titles.

```{python}
#| warning: false
#| fig-alt: A precision-recall curve drawn by hand as a step line

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

import maidr  #<<

X, y = make_classification(
    n_samples=600, n_informative=4, weights=[0.8], random_state=0
)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=0)
scores = LogisticRegression(max_iter=500).fit(X_train, y_train).decision_function(X_test)
precision, recall, _ = precision_recall_curve(y_test, scores)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.step(recall, precision, where="post")
ax.set_xlabel("Recall")  #<<
ax.set_ylabel("Precision")  #<<
ax.set_title("A precision-recall curve drawn by hand")

plt.show()  #<<
```

The precision-recall curves `maidr.keras.plot_pr_curve()` and
`maidr.read_tensorboard_pr_curves()` draw are read the same way; see the
[Keras](../examples-keras.qmd) and [TensorBoard](../examples-tensorboard.qmd)
galleries.
